title: Your first real test, and why assertions matter

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 5 - TypeScript - Arrow functions, `async`, and reading `import`

Every Playwright test is written in **TypeScript**, a programming language that adds types to
JavaScript. This lesson teaches the parts of TypeScript that every test uses. By the end of it, you
will be able to:

- store a value in a variable, and print it
- write a function, and an arrow function
- explain what `async` and `await` do
- read the first two lines of every test file

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | The parts of TypeScript that every Playwright test uses. |
| **Goals** | Store and print values, write functions and arrow functions, explain `async` and `await`, and read an `import` line. |
| **Tools** | `const`, arrow functions, `async` and `await`, destructuring, and `import`. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right. The Console tab shows what your code prints. |
| **Key takeaway** | Put `await` before every step that takes time, inside a function marked `async`. |

## How to run the examples

Select **Load into editor** on an example, then select **Run**. The **Console** tab below the editor
shows everything that the code prints. Each run starts from the beginning, so a value from an earlier
run is never kept.

## Values, variables, and `console.log`

A **value** is a piece of data, such as the number `25` or the text `'Leela'`. A piece of text is
called a **string**, and it is written between quotes. A **variable** is a name that holds a value.
You create one with `const`, which means that the name always holds the same value. You will also
see `let`, which allows the value to change later.

In TypeScript, you can also state the **type** of a variable, meaning the kind of value it holds.
`: string` means text, and `: number` means a number. `console.log` prints a value in the Console
tab.

The example below creates two variables and prints them:

```ts
const name: string = 'Leela';
const age: number = 30;

console.log(name);
console.log(age + 1);
console.log(`Hello, ${name}`);
```

**Output**

```output
Leela
31
Hello, Leela
```

**Explanation:** `age + 1` is calculated before it is printed, so the Console shows `31`. The last
string is written between backticks instead of quotes. A string in backticks can include
the value of a variable with `${...}`, so `${name}` becomes `Leela`.

variation.prompt: Write two arrow functions of your own. The first, cube, returns a number multiplied by itself three times, without braces. The second, farewell, takes a name and returns a goodbye message, inside braces. Print the result of each.
Write an async arrow function named slowGoodbye. It waits half a second with wait(500), then returns a goodbye message for the name it is given. Print its result with await.

blocks.text:
## Objects and destructuring

An **object** groups several named values together, between braces. Each named value is a
**property**. You read a property with a dot, so `user.name` is the `name` property of `user`.

**Destructuring** takes properties out of an object by name. You can destructure in the parameters of
a function, by writing the names you need between braces.

The example below destructures a user in the parameters of a function:

```ts
const user = { name: 'Leela', email: 'leela@gmail.com' };
console.log(user.name);

// Take name and email out of the object that the function receives.
const describeUser = ({ name, email }: { name: string; email: string }) =>
  `${name} <${email}>`;

console.log(describeUser(user));
```

**Output**

```output
Leela
Leela <leela@gmail.com>
```

**Explanation:** `user` is an object with two properties. `describeUser` receives the whole object,
and `{ name, email }` takes out the two properties it needs, so the function can use `name` instead of
`user.name`. The part after the colon, `{ name: string; email: string }`, is the type of the object:
it says which properties the object has, and what kind of value each one holds.

Every test uses this shape. Playwright gives each test an object of tools, called **fixtures**, and
the test takes out the one it needs, which is usually `page`:

```ts
test('the login page opens', async ({ page }) => {
  // Use page here.
});
```

The test is an arrow function. It is marked `async` because it uses `await` for Playwright's actions,
and `({ page })` takes the `page` fixture out of the object that Playwright gives it.

// Write describePlace here, with { city, country } in its parameters.

// Print describePlace({ city: 'Hyderabad', country: 'India' }).

variation.prompt: Write a one-line arrow function named describePlace. It destructures city and country from the object it receives, and returns them as one string, such as 'Hyderabad, India'. Call it and print the result.

blocks.text:
## Arrays

An **array** is a list of values between square brackets. `USERS[0]` is the first item of the
`USERS` list, because counting starts at 0, and `USERS.length` is how many items it holds.

The example below creates an array of two names, and prints the first name and the length:

```ts
const names = ['Leela', 'Katy'];
console.log(names[0], names.length);
```

**Output**

```output
Leela 2
```

**Explanation:** `names[0]` is `'Leela'`, because the first item is at position 0, so the second
item, `'Katy'`, is at position 1. `names.length` is 2, the number of items, not the last position.
This is why `USERS[1]` in [Day 5 - Implementation](/learn/w1/d5/p3) is the second user, Katy.

## Reading `import`

A **package** is code that someone else wrote and published, and that npm installs in your project.
You met `package.json`, which lists your project's packages, in
[Day 3 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d3/p2). An `import` line takes named values out of a package, so
that your file can use them.

Every test file in your project starts with this line:

```ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

**Explanation:** The line takes two values, `test` and `expect`, out of the package
`@playwright/test`. `test` creates a test, and `expect` checks a result.
[Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) uses both. The editor here provides `launch()` and `show()` for you,
so you write this line only in the test files in your own project.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Used braces without `return` | The function gives back `undefined`, which means no value | Add `return`, or remove the braces for a single step. |
| Left out `await` before a step that takes time | A `Promise { <pending> }`, or the next step runs too early | Put `await` before the step. |
| Used `await` in a function without `async` | An error saying that `await` is only allowed in async functions | Put `async` before the parameters of the function. |
`const square = (n: number) => n * n;` contains no `return`. Why does it still return a value?

options: An arrow function always returns the value of the last line inside it.
Without braces, the single step after `=>` is returned.
TypeScript adds a `return` to every function that does not have one.
checkpoint.explanation: An arrow function without braces has exactly one step, and its value is returned automatically. With braces, you must write `return` yourself, or the function gives back `undefined`.

blocks.text: You write `console.log(slowGreet('Katy'))` without `await`. What does the Console show?

options: The greeting, printed after the function has finished waiting for one second
An error, because `await` is always required before calling an async function
`Promise { <pending> }`, because the result is not ready yet
checkpoint.explanation: An async function returns a Promise at once. Without `await`, the code prints the Promise itself, before its result is ready. With `await`, the code waits for the result, and prints the greeting.

blocks.text: In `test('name', async ({ page }) => { ... })`, what does `({ page })` do?

options: It takes the `page` fixture out of the object Playwright gives it.
It opens a new browser tab for the test, and gives that tab the name `page`.
It declares an empty variable named `page`, which the test fills in later on.
checkpoint.explanation: Playwright gives every test one object that holds its fixtures. Destructuring in the parameters takes out the fixtures that you name, so you write `page` instead of a longer name.

blocks.text:
- `const` creates a variable, and `console.log` prints a value.
- An arrow function without braces returns its value. With braces, it needs `return`.
- A **Promise** stands for a result that is not ready yet. `await` waits for it, inside an `async` function.
- **Destructuring** takes properties out of an object by name, as `({ page })` does in every test.
- `import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test'` starts every test file in your project.

## What's next

[Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) uses these parts of the language to write your first real test, with
a check that decides whether the test passes.

parts.title: Your first real test, and why assertions matter

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 5 - Fundamentals - Your first real test, and why assertions matter

In [Day 1 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d1/p2), you read that automation reports only whether a test
passed or failed, against a check that a person wrote. In this lesson, you see what happens when a
test has no check: it passes even when the feature does not work. Then you add a check, and watch the
test fail as it should.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Your first real test, and why a test needs an assertion. |
| **Goals** | Watch a test pass with a wrong password because it checks nothing, then add an assertion and watch the test fail. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1), for arrow functions, `async`, and `import`. |
| **Tools** | `test`, `expect`, `toHaveURL`, and `toBeVisible`. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right for the first example, then your own project for the real tests. |
| **Key takeaway** | A test without an assertion passes whether or not the feature works. |

variation.prompt: Add a step that fails when the sign-in fails. After the click, add await page.waitForURL('**/dashboard', { timeout: 5000 }). This waits up to five seconds for the dashboard to open, and stops the code with an error if it does not. Run the code, and read the error in the Console tab. Then change the password to Leela@123, and run it again.

blocks.text:
## How the assertion works

The line that makes the difference is:

```ts
await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);
```

`expect(page)` says what to check, and `toHaveURL` says what it should be. `/dashboard/` is a
**regular expression**, a pattern for text, which here means "an address that contains `dashboard`".

Playwright's assertions **retry automatically**. `toHaveURL` checks the address again and again, for
up to five seconds, until it matches. If it still does not match after five seconds, the assertion
fails. This means that the assertion also works when the dashboard takes a moment to open.

A good assertion checks the **result** of the steps, not only that the steps ran. For a correct
password, both of these assertions check a result:

```ts
await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);
await expect(page.getByText('Leela')).toBeVisible();
```

The first checks that the dashboard opened, and the second checks that it shows the user's name. For
a wrong password, the result to check is the message:

```ts
await expect(page.getByText('Please Enter Valid Credentials')).toBeVisible();
```

## Best practices

- Give every test at least one assertion that fails when the feature does not work.
- Check the result of the steps, such as the page that opens or the text that appears.
- Watch every new test fail once. Change one value, such as the password, and confirm that the test
  fails. A test that you have never seen fail may not be checking anything.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Wrote a test with no assertion | The test always passes, whether or not the feature works | Add an assertion that checks the result. |
| Checked something that is always on the page | The test passes, even when the steps did not work | Check something that appears only after the steps work, such as the dashboard address. |
| Left out `await` before `expect` | The test can finish before the check is done | Put `await` before every `expect` that checks the page. |
| Used a locator that matches several elements | `strict mode violation: ... resolved to 2 elements` | A locator must match exactly one element. Use text that appears once on the page, or add `.first()` to the locator. |
Both tests type the same wrong password. Why does the first one pass?

options: The website accepted the wrong password, so the sign-in worked.
The test has no assertion, so nothing could fail.
Playwright reports a failed sign-in as a warning, not a failure.
checkpoint.explanation: The sign-in failed in both tests, and the website showed an error message. The first test filled in two fields and selected a button, and each of those steps worked. Nothing checked the result, so the test passed.

blocks.text: Which assertion proves that a correct password signed the user in?

options: `await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' })).toBeVisible()`
`await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/)`, after the click
A check that `click()` finished without an error
checkpoint.explanation: Only a successful sign-in opens the dashboard. The Login button is visible before any sign-in, so checking it proves nothing. A click that finishes proves only that the button could be selected.

blocks.text: You have written a new test, and it passes. What should you do next?

options: Keep it as it is, because a passing test needs no changes.
Run it several more times, to be sure that it passes every time.
Change one value, such as the password, and confirm that it fails.
checkpoint.explanation: A test is useful only if it fails when the feature does not work. Changing one value and watching the test fail proves that its assertions check something.

blocks.text:
- An **assertion** compares what happened with what should have happened, and fails the test if they differ.
- A test without an assertion passes whether or not the feature works.
- Check the result of the steps, such as the dashboard address or the name of the user.
- Assertions retry for up to five seconds before they fail.
- Watch every new test fail once, to prove that it checks something.

## What's next

[Implementation](/learn/w1/d5/p3) takes these sign-in steps, and places them in one piece of code
that every test can use.

parts.title: The same login, with a little structure

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 5 - Implementation - The same login, with a little structure

Both tests in [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) repeat the same sign-in steps. In this lesson, you place
those steps in one piece of code, called a **page object**, which every test can use. You do every
step in VS Code and in its integrated terminal, in your own project.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Writing the sign-in steps once, in a page object that every test can use. |
| **Goals** | Explain what a class, a constructor, and a method are, and use one page object in two tests that expect opposite results. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2), where you wrote the sign-in tests. |
| **Tools** | A class with `constructor`, `readonly`, and `this`, and `new` to make an object from it. |
| **Environment** | VS Code and its integrated terminal, in your project folder, then the editor on the right. |
| **Scope** | This lesson introduces page objects. A later lesson covers the Page Object Model in full. |
| **Key takeaway** | A page object performs the steps, and the test makes the assertions. |

## Why repeated steps are a problem

Imagine fifty tests that each find the email field with `page.getByPlaceholder('Enter Email')`. If
the website changes the placeholder text, you have to change the same line in fifty places. If the
line is written once, in one place, you change it once.

## Classes, in brief

A **class** is a template for an object. It lists the properties that each object made from it has,
and the functions that it can run. A function that belongs to a class is called a **method**. Four
words appear in every class that this course uses:

| Word | What it means |
|---|---|
| `constructor` | A method that runs once, when an object is made from the class. It sets the properties. |
| `this` | The object itself, inside its own methods. `this.page` is the object's `page` property. |
| `new` | Makes an object from a class, as in `new LoginPage(page)`. |
| `readonly` | Marks a property that is set once in the constructor, and never changed afterwards. |

## Step 2: Run the tests

In the integrated terminal, run:

```bash
npx playwright test tests/login-page.spec.ts --project=chromium
```

**Output**

```output
Running 2 tests using 2 workers
  2 passed (7.4s)
```

**Explanation:** Both tests used the same `signIn` method, and both passed. One test expected the
dashboard, and the other expected the error message. Your time and your number of workers may be
different.

## Why the class contains no assertions

The class performs the steps, and the tests decide what the correct result is. That is why one class
serves both tests here, although they expect opposite results. If `signIn` checked for the dashboard
itself, the second test could not use it, because a wrong password never opens the dashboard.

A class like this one is called a page object, and a set of page objects for a website follows the
**Page Object Model**. A later lesson covers it in full.

variation.prompt: Use the same kind of class in the editor, to sign in as Katy. The template contains the class, without its types. Make a LoginPage with new, sign in with USERS[1].email and USERS[1].password, wait for the dashboard with page.waitForURL('**/dashboard'), and show a screenshot.

blocks.text:
## What a reviewer looks for

- Each locator is written once, in the constructor of the page object.
- Methods are named for what a user does, such as `signIn`.
- The page object performs steps, and the tests make every assertion.
Why does `LoginPage` contain no assertions?

options: Assertions can be written only inside a test, never inside a class.
So that tests expecting opposite results can share it.
Because the class runs before Playwright has opened the page.
checkpoint.explanation: One test expects the dashboard, and the other expects an error message. If `signIn` checked for the dashboard itself, the second test could not use it. The class performs the steps, and each test decides what the correct result is.

blocks.text: The website changes the placeholder of its email field. How many lines do you change?

options: One line, in the constructor of `LoginPage`
One line in each test that signs in
Every line that calls `signIn`
checkpoint.explanation: The constructor is the only place that finds the email field. Every test uses `signIn`, and `signIn` uses the locator that the constructor stored, so one change updates every test.

blocks.text:
- A **class** is a template for objects. Its **constructor** sets the properties, and its **methods** perform steps.
- A **page object** finds the elements of one page once, and names the steps, such as `signIn`.
- A page object contains no assertions. The tests decide what the correct result is.
- When the website changes, you update the page object, not every test.

## What's next

[Practice](/learn/w1/d5/p4) has you write a test of your own, see the missing-assertion problem for
yourself, and build a small page object.

parts.title: Practice: your first test, and the assertions gap

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 5 - Practice - Your first test, and the assertions gap

These three problems use the test shape and the assertions from [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2), and
the page object from [Implementation](/learn/w1/d5/p3). You write and run each test in your own
project.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Three problems about your first tests, from Beginner level to Advanced, to complete Week 1. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) for assertions, and [Implementation](/learn/w1/d5/p3) for page objects. |
| **Environment** | Your own project for the tests, and the editor on the right for your answers. |

## How to answer

Select **Start this in the editor** to open a template for a problem, and write your answer on the
lines that start with `//`. Select **Reveal solution** to compare it with a model answer.

## When you are done

You have now completed Week 1. You can explain why teams automate tests, set up a project, run tests
and read their results, find elements with locators, and write a test whose assertion decides whether
it passes. [Week 2 - Day 1 - Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d1/p2) continues from here.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** A test that signs in as Katy, with assertions from the start. Katy's email is
`katy@gmail.com`, and her password is `Katy@12354`. In the `tests` folder, create
`practice-login.spec.ts`, as in [Day 4 - Implementation](/learn/w1/d4/p3), write the test, and run
it with `npx playwright test tests/practice-login.spec.ts --project=chromium`. Then change the
password to a wrong one, run the same command again, and read how it fails.

**Where.** In VS Code and its integrated terminal. Copy your test and the two results into the
editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** The first run reports `1 passed`, and the run with the wrong
password reports `1 failed`.

**Hint.** Start from the second test in [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2), and check both the address
and the user's name.

**What to build.** The missing-assertion problem from [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2), from the
beginning. In the `tests` folder, create `practice-gap.spec.ts`, with one test that signs in as
Leela with a wrong password and has no assertion. Run it with
`npx playwright test tests/practice-gap.spec.ts --project=chromium`. Then add
`await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);` as the last line of the same test, and run the same
command again.

**Where.** In VS Code and its integrated terminal. Write the two results, and one sentence about
what changed, in the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** The same test reported `1 passed` the first time and `1 failed` the
second time.

**What to build.** A page object in a file of its own, and a test that uses it. In the `tests`
folder:

1. Create `login-page.ts`, with a `LoginPage` class that has two methods. `signIn(email, password)`
   performs the sign-in steps, as in [Implementation](/learn/w1/d5/p3). `signedInName(name)` returns
   the text of the element that shows the user's name, with
   `await this.page.getByText(name).innerText()`.
2. Start the class with `export`, so that another file can import it.
3. Create `practice-page-object.spec.ts`, with one test that imports `LoginPage` from
   `'./login-page'`, signs in as Leela, and checks that `signedInName('Leela')` returns `'Leela'`.

**Where.** In VS Code and its integrated terminal. Copy both files into the editor, using the
template.

**How you will know it worked.** The test reports `1 passed`, and every locator is in
`login-page.ts`, not in the test file.

**Hint.** Name the page object file `login-page.ts`, without `.spec`. [Day 4 - Implementation](/learn/w1/d4/p3)
explains why that matters. Four things in this problem are new. `export` before `class` lets another
file use the class. In `import { LoginPage } from './login-page'`, the `./` means the same folder as
the test file. `innerText()` reads the text inside an element, as a string. `expect(x).toBe('Leela')`
compares two strings, and needs no `await`, because there is no page to wait for.
